title: India Opens One-Time Window for NRIs to Disclose Undisclosed Foreign Assets
excerpt: The FAST-DS 2026 scheme gives eligible taxpayers a six-month window to voluntarily declare overseas assets up to ₹5 crore, with immunity from prosecution under the Black Money Act.
body:
• The FAST-DS 2026 scheme provides a one-time, six-month window for taxpayers to voluntarily disclose undisclosed foreign assets or income, with immunity from prosecution under the Black Money Act
  • Category A covers those who failed to disclose overseas income or assets up to ₹1 crore — they pay 60% of the value (30% tax plus 30% additional charge) for full immunity
  • Category B covers those who paid tax on income but didn't declare the acquired foreign asset (up to ₹5 crore) — they pay a flat fee of ₹1 lakh for immunity from penalty and prosecution
  • The scheme targets returning NRIs, tech employees with foreign ESOPs/RSUs, students, and young professionals who may have missed Schedule FA disclosures

India's government has introduced a one-time foreign asset disclosure scheme that could offer significant relief to Non-Resident Indians returning home, tech professionals holding overseas stock options, and anyone who has inadvertently failed to report foreign assets in their Indian tax returns.

What Is FAST-DS 2026?

Announced by Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in the Union Budget 2026, the Foreign Assets of Small Taxpayers — Disclosure Scheme (FAST-DS) creates a six-month window for eligible taxpayers to voluntarily declare previously undisclosed foreign bank accounts, investments, ESOPs, RSUs, and other overseas assets. In exchange, declarants receive full immunity from prosecution and penalties under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015.

https://x.com/EconomicTimes/status/2088511167840854325

Under existing tax law, all foreign assets must be disclosed annually in the FA Schedule of ITR-2 or ITR-3 — even if they generate no income. Failure to report, even without any tax evasion, can attract a ₹10 lakh annual penalty and up to seven years of imprisonment under the Black Money Act.

Two Categories of Taxpayers

The scheme applies to two distinct categories:

Category A covers taxpayers who failed to disclose both their overseas income and assets. The limit for undisclosed income or assets is up to ₹1 crore. These declarants must pay 30% of the fair market value of the undisclosed asset (or 30% of undisclosed income) as tax, plus an additional 30% as a charge in lieu of penalty — a total of 60% of the asset's value. In return, they receive complete immunity from prosecution.

Category B covers taxpayers who did declare their overseas income and paid the due tax, but failed to report the foreign asset itself in Schedule FA. The proposed limit is up to ₹5 crore. These taxpayers receive immunity from both penalty and prosecution by paying a flat fee of just ₹1 lakh. If the same asset went undisclosed across multiple years, the fee applies only for the first year of non-disclosure — after that, the asset is considered permanently regularized.

Who Should Pay Attention

The scheme was designed with specific groups in mind: returning NRIs who maintained foreign bank accounts funded through legitimate channels like the Liberalised Remittance Scheme; tech employees at multinational companies holding foreign ESOPs or RSUs through overseas brokerage accounts; students who studied abroad and may still hold foreign accounts; and young professionals who relocated and didn't realize the reporting requirements applied to them.

"To address practical issues of small taxpayers like students, young professionals, tech employees, relocated NRIs, and such others, I propose to introduce a one-time 6-month foreign asset disclosure scheme for these taxpayers."

— Nirmala Sitharaman, Finance Minister of India

For many in this group, the non-disclosure was inadvertent — they paid taxes on their income but simply didn't know about Schedule FA requirements. Without this scheme, a returning NRI with a ₹2 crore foreign bank account that was legitimately funded but not reported could face ₹10 lakh in penalties per assessment year across multiple years. Under FAST-DS Category B, the same situation resolves with a single ₹1 lakh payment.

The Compliance Push

The Income Tax Department recently launched a Foreign Assets Information report on its e-filing portal, allowing taxpayers to view what overseas asset data the department already has. The feature is seen as a precursor to the formal notification of FAST-DS — giving taxpayers a chance to identify gaps before the disclosure window officially opens.

The scheme has been enacted through the Finance Bill 2026 but will become operational only after the government issues a formal notification in the Official Gazette with the specific six-month timeline. Once notified, declarants will need to obtain a certified valuation, submit a digital declaration, make the required payment, and receive an official certificate of clearance.

For NRIs and diaspora professionals with any foreign financial footprint, the message is clear: regularize now at a defined cost, or risk discovery later at a far steeper one.
nri_angle: The scheme directly targets returning NRIs, tech professionals with foreign ESOPs, and students who may have failed to report overseas bank accounts and investments in their Indian tax returns.
